```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r packages, message=FALSE}
library("naboer")
library("dplyr")
library("tibble")
library("mgcv")
library("units")

have_spatial <- requireNamespace("sf", quietly = TRUE)
have_cubble <- have_spatial && requireNamespace("cubble", quietly = TRUE)

if (have_spatial) {
  library("sf")
}
if (have_cubble) {
  library("cubble")
}
```

Use a distance window to assess observations individually while leaving nearby
observations out of the training data. Use spatial blocks to assess all
observations in an area together. You can also add a distance buffer around the
observations in each assessment block.

Install `sf` to work with station geometries. A standard naboer installation
includes `units` to specify distances. For raster data, take the locations and
values of the cells used for modelling and represent those locations as `sf`
points with the raster's coordinate reference system. If you already have fold
memberships, supply their row numbers with `custom_folds()`.

## Choose smoothness for spatial data

Suppose you want to map daily maximum temperature where weather stations are
sparse. When choosing how smooth the map should be, you can score the prediction
at each station after leaving out that station and nearby stations. Here we use
records from Victoria and New South Wales, Australia, on 15 January 2018. The
data come from the Global Historical Climatology Network Daily. Install
`cubble` to use its copy of the data and run this example. [Data documentation](https://huizezhang-sherry.github.io/cubble/reference/climate-data.html),
[cubble paper](https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v110i07).

Use `dplyr` to keep one row per station and retain stations with both
temperature and elevation recorded.

```{r weather-stations, eval=have_cubble}
weather <- historical_tmax |>
  face_temporal() |>
  filter(date == as.Date("2018-01-15")) |>
  unfold(long, lat, elev) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  filter(is.finite(tmax), is.finite(elev))
```

Project station locations onto the Australian Albers grid (EPSG:3577) so we can
use distances in a common coordinate system. Save easting and northing in
kilometres as predictors for the model.

```{r project-stations, eval=have_cubble}
weather_points <- st_as_sf(weather, coords = c("long", "lat"), crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(3577)
coordinates <- st_coordinates(weather_points) / 1000
weather_points$east_km <- coordinates[, "X"]
weather_points$north_km <- coordinates[, "Y"]
```

Make one fold per station. Each fold scores the target station and leaves that
station and all stations within 100 km out of the training data. The radius
illustrates a prediction task with few nearby stations. For your own analysis,
choose the distance to reflect where you expect to make predictions or how far
residual dependence extends.

```{r weather-neighbourhoods, eval=have_cubble}
weather_folds <- neighbourhoods(weather_points,
  spatial = spatial_window(set_units(100, "km"))
)
range(lengths(omission_indices(weather_folds)))
```

Fit temperature as a function of elevation and a smooth surface over easting
and northing. `as_nei()` supplies the omitted and scored rows to mgcv's `gam()`
for quadratic neighbourhood cross-validation (QNCV). The Gaussian model here
has quadratic loss, so QNCV gives the same smoothing criterion as neighbourhood
cross-validation (NCV). Use `fold_data()` so the model data have the row order
expected by the exported indices. The folds determine how `gam()` chooses the
smoothing parameter. The returned model uses all the rows at the chosen
smoothness.

```{r spatial-ncv-fit, eval=have_cubble}
weather_data <- fold_data(weather_folds)
weather_formula <- tmax ~ elev + s(east_km, north_km, k = 20)
spatial_fit <- gam(weather_formula,
  data = weather_data, method = "QNCV",
  nei = as_nei(weather_folds, data = weather_data),
  na.action = na.fail
)
```

Fit the same model with `method = "QNCV"` and leave `nei` unset to use mgcv's
default leave-one-out criterion. Compare the selected smoothing parameters and
the effective degrees of freedom, which measure how flexible each fitted
surface is. In this example the spatial neighbourhoods select a smoother
surface, with about 10 effective degrees of freedom compared with about 14.5
under leave-one-out.

```{r compare-spatial-fits, eval=have_cubble}
loo_fit <- gam(weather_formula,
  data = weather_data, method = "QNCV", na.action = na.fail
)
tibble(
  criterion = c("Leave-one-out", "Spatial neighbourhoods"),
  smoothing_parameter = c(unname(loo_fit$sp), unname(spatial_fit$sp)),
  effective_degrees_of_freedom = c(
    summary(loo_fit)$s.table[1, "edf"],
    summary(spatial_fit)$s.table[1, "edf"]
  )
)
```

Draw the fitted spatial QNCV surface at the median station elevation. The
contours show predicted maximum temperature in °C, and the dots are station
locations. `too.far` controls which predictions appear in the figure. It masks
areas far from any station after scaling each plot axis to run from 0 to 1.

```{r plot-spatial-ncv, eval=have_cubble, fig.width=6, fig.height=5, dev.args=list(bg="white"), fig.alt="Contour map of fitted maximum temperatures across southeastern Australia, with weather station locations marked as dots."}
vis.gam(spatial_fit,
  view = c("east_km", "north_km"),
  cond = list(elev = median(weather_data$elev)),
  type = "response", plot.type = "contour", n.grid = 60, too.far = 0.1,
  contour.col = "grey15",
  xlab = "Easting (km)", ylab = "Northing (km)",
  main = "Fitted temperature (°C)"
)
points(weather_data$east_km, weather_data$north_km, pch = 20)
```

## Assessing individual sites

Define a 200-metre window. You can specify the distance before supplying any
geometry.

```{r site-window}
site_window <- spatial_window(set_units(200, "m"))
```

Create six sites on a straight line in a projected coordinate reference
system (CRS) with coordinates in metres.

```{r sites, eval=have_spatial}
sites <- st_as_sf(
  tibble(
    site = letters[1:6], east = c(0, 100, 500, 1000, 2000, 3000), north = 0
  ),
  coords = c("east", "north"), crs = 32632
)
```

Use the window to construct folds. Each fold assesses one site and omits that
site and any others within 200 metres when fitting the model.

```{r make-site-folds, eval=have_spatial}
site_folds <- neighbourhoods(sites, spatial = site_window)
```

Compare the first three folds. Sites `a` and `b` are 100 metres apart, so both
are omitted from training when either is assessed. Site `c` is more than 200
metres from every other site, so its fold omits only site `c`.

```{r site-folds, eval=have_spatial}
as_tibble(site_folds, folds = 1:3)
```

Distance windows use the original geometries, including lines and polygons.
Supply valid, non-empty geometries with a declared CRS. For longitude and
latitude, `naboer` uses the current spherical or ellipsoidal distance setting in
`sf`, as selected by `sf_use_s2()`.

Distance windows and block assignments use the stored coordinates. If you want
your design to use rounded locations, round the coordinates before constructing
the folds. `fold_data()` preserves any `sf` precision attribute on the input.

## Assessing spatial blocks

Split the sites into 500-metre square blocks and assess the observations in one
occupied block at a time. The `origin` fixes the grid to the same anchor if you
repeat the analysis on a subset of these sites in the same CRS.

```{r blocks, eval=have_spatial}
blocks <- spatial_folds(sites, size = set_units(500, "m"), origin = c(0, 0))
```

Observations on either side of a block boundary can be close together. Add a
100-metre buffer to omit nearby observations from training. The `n_buffer`
column counts observations left out of training solely because of this buffer.

```{r buffered-blocks, eval=have_spatial}
buffered <- buffer_folds(
  blocks, spatial = spatial_window(set_units(100, "m"))
)
as_tibble(buffered)
```

Square cell boundaries pass through `origin = c(x, y)`. With
`shape = "hexagonal"`, a cell is centred on the anchor and `size` is the distance
between opposite edges. The default anchor is calculated from the data extent.

You can also supply your own polygons with `regions`. By default, an observation
that intersects several cells or touches a shared boundary goes in the first
matching cell. Generated grids are ordered by row from south to north, with
cells in each row ordered west to east. Custom regions follow their supplied
order. If the interiors of custom regions overlap, use `assignment` to name a
column giving the region row number for each observation. Each assigned region
must intersect its observation. The observations keep their original geometries.

To generate blocks from longitude and latitude, `spatial_folds()` projects the
data onto a local azimuthal equidistant projection centred on the study area.
For large study areas, supply an appropriate projected `grid_crs`. You must set
`grid_crs` if the longitude range exceeds 180 degrees, as can happen where a
study area crosses the 180th meridian. Geographic distance windows work across
this boundary. Block widths are measured in the grid's projection, so their
surface distances may vary across a large study area.

Before creating a grid, `naboer` checks its estimated memory use against the
`naboer.max_bytes` option, which defaults to 1 GiB. A larger cell size or a
smaller study extent reduces the number of cells.

## Repeated station observations

Suppose each site has one observation per day for ten days. Use `site` as the
series key and `date` as the time index.

```{r station-observations, eval=have_spatial}
observations <- sites[rep(seq_len(nrow(sites)), each = 10), ]
observations$date <- rep(as.Date("2024-01-01") + 0:9, nrow(sites))
```

Reuse the 200-metre spatial window and add a one-day window on either side of
the assessment date. With `combine = "intersection"`, a record is omitted from
training if it is close in both space and time. With `combine = "union"`,
closeness in either dimension is sufficient.

```{r joint-window, eval=have_spatial}
day_window <- temporal_window(time_span(1, "days"))
joint <- neighbourhoods(
  observations,
  key = site, index = date,
  spatial = site_window, temporal = day_window, combine = "intersection"
)
```

Inspect an assessment on the first day at site `a`, the fifth day at site `b`
and the last day at site `f`. The folds at the nearby sites `a` and `b` omit
records from both sites. The fold at site `f` omits records from that site alone.

```{r joint-folds, eval=have_spatial}
as_tibble(joint, folds = c(1, 15, 60))
```

Temporal windows can span stations by default. Use `within = "key"` to limit
the temporal window to each station, or `.by` if both spatial and temporal
windows should be confined to independent groups. Distances between fixed
stations are reused across dates. If sites move, each observation's recorded
geometry determines its neighbours.

To assess blocks instead of individual observations, use
`spatiotemporal_folds()`. `mode = "crossed"` assesses the observations in a
spatial block during a time block. `mode = "space"` holds out spatial blocks
across all dates, and `mode = "time"` holds out time blocks across stations.

## Cubble

For spatiotemporal data, use a cubble to keep measurements linked to their site
locations. Put the measured values in a table with a site and date for each
record, then link them to the site geometries.

```{r make-cubble, eval=have_cubble}
values <- st_drop_geometry(observations)
values$value <- seq_len(nrow(values))
cube <- make_cubble(
  spatial = sites, temporal = values, key = site, index = date
)
```

`neighbourhoods()` reads the key and index from the cubble. Apply the same
windows as before, then inspect the data in the row order used by the folds.

```{r cubble-folds, eval=have_cubble}
cube_folds <- neighbourhoods(
  cube, spatial = site_window, temporal = day_window, combine = "intersection"
)
head(fold_data(cube_folds))
```

You can pass a nested spatial cubble or its long temporal form. In both cases,
`fold_data()` returns one row per measurement with its original site geometry,
including polygons. If the site data contain several geometry columns, the
design uses the active geometry. The `naboer_source` attribute identifies the
original site row and position within the series for nested data, or the
original observation row for long data. Measurements with missing coordinates
remain available for purely temporal folds.

If several columns together identify a series, create a combined key before
constructing a cubble. With an `sf` object or tibble, you can select the
separate columns directly with `key`.
